summary:
The Earth Information Jukebox is a project developed by Team PROMPT PILOTS for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Our idea is to make Earth science more accessible by turning visual patterns from NASA Scientific Visualization Studio (SVS) imagery into interactive audio experiences.

The application currently features three NASA experiences: Ocean Currents and Temperature (SVS 3912), Lightning Events Detected from the ISS (SVS 5011), and Atmospheric Aerosols (SVS 5572). Using visual feature processing and the Web Audio API, we transform selected image features into sound, allowing people to explore Earth phenomena in a different way.

We especially want to make this experience useful for blind and low-vision users, while also supporting students, educators, and anyone interested in Earth science. The application includes optional voice guidance, voice commands, keyboard navigation, and screen-reader support.

Built with React, TypeScript, Vite, and Express.js, this project combines technology, creativity, and accessibility.

Currently, the audio is generated from visual features in NASA imagery rather than directly from underlying numerical measurements. In the future, we aim to integrate verified scientific datasets, add more experiences, and improve accessibility through user testing.

Our goal is simple: to help more people experience the wonders of our planet, one sound at a time.
details:
The Earth Information Jukebox is an accessibility-focused web application that gives people a different way to explore and experience Earth science through sound.

Our project takes visual patterns from NASA Scientific Visualization Studio (SVS) imagery and transforms selected image features into audio using sonification techniques. Users can explore three different NASA experiences: Ocean Currents and Temperature, Lightning Events Detected from the ISS, and Atmospheric Aerosols. The application processes visual features, maps them to audio parameters, and generates sounds through the Web Audio API. Users can interact with the experience using playback controls such as play, pause, stop, replay, and volume adjustment.

One of the main goals of this project is to make Earth science more accessible, particularly for people who are blind or have low vision. Instead of relying entirely on visual information, users can explore scientific visualizations through audio. The project can also be useful for students, educators, and anyone curious about our planet. Accessibility features include optional voice guidance, voice commands, keyboard navigation, and screen-reader support.

We developed the application using React, TypeScript, and Vite for the frontend, Express.js for the backend, and the Web Audio API for sound generation.

What makes our idea creative is the way it connects NASA's Earth science visualizations with sound, turning visual exploration into an interactive listening experience. During development, we considered accessibility, ease of use, meaningful sound mapping, technical reliability, and the importance of presenting NASA content responsibly.

We also recognize an important limitation: our current audio experiences are generated from visual features in NASA imagery, not directly from the underlying numerical scientific measurements. We aim to improve this by integrating verified NASA datasets in future versions.

Through this project, we hope to make Earth science more inclusive and inspire people to explore our planet in a new way — not just by seeing it, but by hearing it.
